epigraph: I left my whole soul 356 metres beneath the sea
intro: I wanted to create a story about the underwater world and the depths of the sea. Hence rapture of the deep: a scuba-diving accident that generally happens below 30 metres, when excess nitrogen acts on the nervous system and disturbs the diver’s behaviour.
The diver is overcome by narcosis, whose effects can be avoided by returning to the surface at the first signs of rapture. To get round the problem, many divers mix different breathing gases.
So it is that Paul, my protagonist, recounts his descent into the furthest reaches of his own rapture, and we discover the events that overwhelmed him on the way down.

paragraphs: An altered state usually comes down to too much alcohol or drugs, to losing control of situations and of yourself. For me, the altered state is rapture, and above all rapture of the deep, the kind that flooded through me and took hold of my whole being.

I have always been in love with the underwater world. I started swimming very young, encouraged by my parents, and at 15 I discovered scuba diving. Like any self-respecting child, I idolised Lloyd Bridges, the American actor from the series Sea Hunt, who solved murders and took on the dangers of the sea. My dream was to be like him, to push myself at every moment while doing something I loved. But diving was also another way of swimming, another way to decompress. Then, throughout my studies, my life was ruled by nothing but maths, physics and mechanics. My passions no longer came into it; I quite simply didn’t have the time… Once I had graduated, I realised that what really mattered to me was feeling the water on my skin, being free, swimming, pushing my limits, going ever faster and ever further. It was all I truly wanted, my only dream. Scuba diving can be very dangerous. That is what makes the sport so thrilling, so addictive, so exhilarating.

I leave home with Dag, an adorable border collie. We’re off to Egypt, not for a beach holiday but to take on a challenge. You may have heard of Ahmed Gamal Gabr, an Egyptian combat diver who reached a depth of 332.35 metres in 2014. I could talk about what he has achieved for hours!

Anyway, here I am, on my way to try and beat his world record in the very spot where he made his descent. The terrain there is dramatic, both above sea level and below it, forming an underwater valley, which makes it a particularly interesting place to dive. It’s in the Dahab area that I can at last train for a dive to 350 metres, even though I have never been anywhere near that deep in my life. In theory, I should be able to come back up alive and in one piece. Only after several days of physical training, practice runs and emergency drills will I be able to consider going down into the tunnel.

When I get to Egypt, I’m given a warm welcome in Dahab. The people there are incredibly kind and help me a great deal with my preparations for the big day. My dog comes along to every training session and waits for me, running up and down the sand. He looks as if he’s worried about me. And yet he knows my passion and often comes with me when I dive.

Through training, I have been able to discover and get used to the environment I’m about to plunge into. Visibility is poor, and there are strong currents in the first 30 metres, so it takes me a lot of dives to familiarise myself with the terrain and the currents. Each session brings new sensations and I’m beginning to feel good.

When at last I felt ready, we had to wait for a weather window suitable for my descent. When you decide to make a dive like this, you can’t leave anything to chance. It’s no gentle stroll, where you can stop and rest until conditions improve. On this descent the slightest problem, however trivial, could kill me. So, with my team of doctors and professionals, I look for the right day, in the right conditions, to set this new adventure in motion.
The window finally opens on 15 September 2021 at 9.26am. At last, the team and I head out to sea to achieve my goal, my dream.

I get ready by digging out the warmest clothes I can find in my suitcase, then join the others on the pontoon. My diving gear has been ready since the day before: never knowing when we would have to leave, I had left it waiting somewhere warm.
I’m torn between excitement, stress, pride, desire and fear at the thought of this descent. Many have died before me, and I can’t really know what is going to happen.

I cut short the words of encouragement on the pontoon and board the boat that will take me to the descent point. A smaller boat is waiting for us there; they have already dropped my lifeline into the water. It’s a lifeline hung with oxygen cylinders, so that I can make my ascent and my decompression stops safely, without straying too far from my reference points.

They put me through some quick concentration tests. Someone stands facing me, arms outstretched, with a ball in each hand, while my own hands are behind my back. They let go of the balls at random and I have to catch them before they hit the ground. My team checks my heart rate and gives me one last short briefing, going over the safety instructions.
And so I’m off, for 14 minutes going down and 16 hours coming back up.

I throw myself into the water. For the start of the descent I’m accompanied by divers, who make sure that I’m not feeling faint, that I’m still responsive and that I feel all right. From 25 metres down, I’m finally alone, with myself and my mind. That leaves just 16 hours and 12 minutes, with only my own mind for company.

For me it’s a moment to reflect on what I have achieved and on what drives me to keep going today and to make this descent. I tell myself it’s more than a record to beat: it’s a personal victory, a way of saying that everything I have done so far has allowed me to realise my childhood dream of being like Lloyd Bridges, a man pushing his limits.

As I pass the 291-metre mark, after only 10 minutes underwater, a strange feeling comes over me. Whoosh: a shadow passes right in front of my eyes. Whoosh, another one. Whoosh, whoosh! It isn’t the first time I’ve felt this and I broadly know how to react, but every episode shows itself differently. The shadows go by without my being able to make out any shape, as if each were an old sheet from the back of a cupboard at your grandparents’ house, flying through the water like a jellyfish, only much faster. Then suddenly, nothing.

I understand at once what is happening. I’m hallucinating. I had been warned of the risks I was taking. I know I mustn’t panic. The first thing I check is my oxygen supply, then my depth, the time and the temperature. To be sure, I decide to start again: oxygen, depth, time, temperature. A flicker of panic brushes against me.

Oxygen, depth, time, temperature. Oxygen, depth, time, temperature. I shake my head to stop the narcosis. With my wits about me again, I see that I have only 59 metres left to beat Ahmed Gamal Gabr’s record. Only 58 now… The one thing occupying my conscious thoughts is beating this record, but the narcosis takes hold again. It feels as if there are explosions all around me. Boom, a bomb; boom, a second. As in a scene from a naval film in which a warship is attacked from the air, objects fall into the water. The water slows the bombs down all around me. I have the nasty impression of being pushed back by the tunnel of water that the falling bombs have carved out around me. I can’t move forward any more, I’m even going backwards, but I know I really mustn’t waste any time: my air is limited, and no one is there to help me if anything goes wrong. I’m all alone with these demons. I grab the lifeline to my right. I know I have to reach at least the cylinder at the next stop down, so as to have enough oxygen to get back up without trouble. After a moment’s thought, I slide one hand down the line, then the other, and lower myself little by little. Even though everything happening around me is only a figment of my imagination, I can’t resist the perception, it’s so real. A few metres further on, I finally reach the air cylinder and check how many metres I have left. This episode has put me behind: there are only 18 metres to go to Ahmed Gamal Gabr’s record, and so 36 to the 350 metres I want to reach. But I quickly understand that the known symptoms of rapture of the deep include hallucinations, which are what I’m experiencing now.
And yet I decide to keep going down, even at the risk of losing my life. I would rather die than return to the surface without this new world record.

All of a sudden, I sense slight movements behind me. An unknown form hurls itself at me and strikes me on the side. I only just have time to catch hold of my lifeline before the creature knocks me about again, one way and then the other. The thing throws me with such force that I can’t collect myself. I can no longer tell up from down, or down from up. Everything is jumbled in my mind, as if my whole body had been replaced by a curling stone, thrown across the ice with skill and strength, and the water had become the two little figures beside it, sweeping the ice with their brooms to send the stone as far as possible across the frozen water. I have barely had time to recover when I have to make a choice, neither considered nor lucid, but crucial: which way to go? Up, down, left, right? I’ll have to choose, because my time is running out. I’ve lost the lifeline. Like a character in an 80s video game, who can only move along lines of code, I set off: right, up, down, left, up, down. I seem to be going deeper. That’s a good start, but so far there is no lifeline in sight. It’s the most important thing of all, for without it there is no salvation. I pick my way between the lines of code towards my final goal. I assume I’m moving towards the lifeline and going down, because my electronic instruments tell me that the depth is increasing, from 314 metres to 316, then 317. In theory, everything is in place for me to reach my goal of 350 metres. Then, suddenly, my memory stops. My brain remembers nothing but this blue, dark and infinite, stretching out everywhere around me as far as the eye can see, above, below, on every side, all this space merging to form the cocoon that wraps around me and carries me off… And yet the further I forge my way through the water, the more tired I feel.

Paul drifts off. As he sinks deeper into the water, the light, like his strength, gradually fades. A tunnel appears. Paul chooses to stop for a moment, even if it means going back up a little so that he can set off again in better shape. Still without his lifeline, he has to rely on his computers to be sure he really is ascending. When he feels better, he pauses. His mind steadied, he decides to resume his descent. The higher the figures climb on his depth gauge, the scarcer and darker the light becomes, until he can hardly make out what is around him, as if a tunnel were closing in on him.

Paul goes deeper and deeper. He carries on; he won’t stop until he reaches his goal. Time passes, the metres mount up, the distance to his goal shrinks. He keeps going regardless. But this is more of a fall than a dive. For without his lifeline, he is lost.

In Paul’s mind, as in the sea around him, the darkness is total. He no longer knows where he is or where he is going. Only his wish to beat the world record still drives him and ties him to the world of the surface, to life. But as rapture of the deep takes hold, that glimmer of lucidity, his goal, grows smaller and smaller, further and further away. It is now no more than a pea in a dark ocean.

It is by sheer chance that his hand brushes the lifeline, and by sheer reflex that he grabs it and starts to haul himself up by the strength of his arms, for his legs no longer obey his clouded brain. As he rises he tries to gather his wits, but his mind stays fogged, as though drawn by the sirens of the infinite deep. The ascent is long, because it takes many decompression stops for his body to readjust to the pressure falling as he rises. The rescue teams are there. They realised something was wrong when the cameras fixed along the lifeline stopped sending images of Paul at regular intervals. At that depth they couldn’t reach him, but as he climbed Paul also drew closer to the rescuers, to the light, to life. He was unconscious when he made the stops and covered the tens of metres that separated him from the open air, stops that were essential to his survival. And he is unconscious when he finally surfaces, after 16 hours and 14 minutes in the endless world of the sea.

When I came round, I learnt that I had beaten the record after all. Not consciously, no. It was my depth gauge that recorded the deepest point of my descent, 356 metres below the surface. But at what cost? This underwater world still haunts me. Every time I close my eyes, I feel myself thrown among the watery ghosts who toy with me as if I were a pinball, firing me in every direction as they please. Even on land, I can’t find up or down any more. The world no longer makes sense, quite literally. I left my sense of balance, of gravity, of reality 356 metres beneath the sea. I will never be able to dive again. But I love swimming and being in the water as much as ever. Only now I take care not to swim too deep, because I know the sirens are waiting for me and calling me, again and again, endlessly.

back: Paul, an experienced swimmer and diver, leaves for Egypt to break a world record, held by an Egyptian combat diver who reached a depth of 332 metres in the open sea. And so Paul sets off, for 14 minutes going down and 16 hours coming back up. In an endless blue tunnel, alone with his mind.
